title: Sixty-Five Squared
statement: For each positive integer $n$, let $a_n = 10^n + 5^n + 2^n + 1$. For how many positive integers $n \le 1000$ is $a_n$ divisible by $4225$?
hints: Before looking at any prime, write $a_n$ as a product of two simpler numbers.

$a_n = (2^n + 1)(5^n + 1)$ and $4225 = 5^2 \cdot 13^2$. For each of the primes $5$ and $13$, decide which of the two factors it divides and for which $n$, using orders modulo that prime, and use lifting the exponent for the squares. Check both factors for each prime.

You should find that $5 \mid 2^n + 1$ exactly when $n \equiv 2 \pmod 4$, with $v_5(2^n + 1) = 1 + v_5(n)$. For $13$, there are two sources: $13 \mid 5^n + 1$ exactly when $n \equiv 2 \pmod 4$, and $13 \mid 2^n + 1$ exactly when $n \equiv 6 \pmod{12}$, and in each case the factor has $13$-adic valuation $1 + v_{13}(n)$. Turn this into a description of the good $n$ by residues, and count.
solution:
We have $a_n = (2^n + 1)(5^n + 1)$ and $4225 = 5^2 \cdot 13^2$.

The prime $5$ does not divide $5^n + 1$. The powers of $2$ modulo $5$ are $2, 4, 3, 1$, so $5 \mid 2^n + 1$ exactly when $n \equiv 2 \pmod 4$. Then $n = 2k$ with $k$ odd, and lifting the exponent gives $v_5(4^k + 1) = v_5(5) + v_5(k) = 1 + v_5(n)$. So $25 \mid a_n$ exactly when $n \equiv 2 \pmod 4$ and $5 \mid n$, that is, $n \equiv 10 \pmod{20}$.

Modulo $13$, $5^2 \equiv -1$, so $13 \mid 5^n + 1$ exactly when $n \equiv 2 \pmod 4$, and then, with $n = 2k$ and $k$ odd, $v_{13}(25^k + 1) = v_{13}(26) + v_{13}(k) = 1 + v_{13}(n)$. Also $2^4 \equiv 3$ and $2^6 \equiv -1$, so $2$ has order $12$ and $13 \mid 2^n + 1$ exactly when $n \equiv 6 \pmod{12}$; then, with $n = 6j$ and $j$ odd, $v_{13}(64^j + 1) = v_{13}(65) + v_{13}(j) = 1 + v_{13}(n)$.

Now let $n \equiv 10 \pmod{20}$. If $3 \mid n$, then $n \equiv 6 \pmod{12}$, both factors are divisible by $13$, and $169 \mid a_n$. If $3 \nmid n$, only $5^n + 1$ is divisible by $13$, and $169 \mid a_n$ exactly when $13 \mid n$. So $4225 \mid a_n$ exactly when $n \equiv 10 \pmod{20}$ and $n$ is divisible by $3$ or by $13$.

Up to $1000$ there are $17$ such $n$ with $n \equiv 30 \pmod{60}$, $4$ with $n \equiv 130 \pmod{260}$, and $1$, namely $390$, in both classes. The answer is $17 + 4 - 1 = 20$.
